questions.q: What is a preferred indifferent in Stoicism?
a: Something you would choose but can accept losing
Something you must avoid no matter the cost
Something that has no moral value at all
Something only a sage is allowed to want
questions.why: Lesson one defines it as an option you prefer if possible but remain content without, such as wealth or health.

questions.q: Which four qualities make up Stoic virtue?
questions.why: Lesson two breaks virtue into self-control, bravery, fairness and wisdom, with wisdom considered the most important.

questions.q: Which part of virtue did the Stoics value most?
questions.why: Lesson two says wisdom was ranked highest because it helps you choose well whatever the circumstances.

questions.q: Which friendship type is based on who people are, not what they share?
questions.why: Lesson three says friendships of the good rest on character rather than business or hobbies, making them the strongest.

questions.q: How should we treat friendships built on usefulness or shared hobbies?
a: As nice to have but not essential to a good life
As the only friendships worth keeping
As more important than family ties
questions.why: The summary says the first two kinds are worth having but should be treated as preferred indifferents.
